Utilizing clarinets only in its Pie Jesu movement, this piece calls for expanded percussion in its last movement, In Paradisum. The Kyrie movement of this piece is the only movement that utilizes Greek, while the rest use originalLatin. Identify this musical setting of the Catholic Mass for the Dead, which was written by Gabriel Fauré.

One of the title figures of this painting has intimate detail on the two brooches that secure his garment at the shoulders, which are depicted next to the jeweled sash that crosses his chest from left to right. That tabard is worn over a white garment with scenes painted on its sleeves, and although the background of this painting is insdistinct, three or four bricks are set out from the wall on the left. The illumination from the left side of this painting highlights the title character's hand on the head of a statue which depicts a bearded blind man. Identify this portrait of a philosopher with his hand on the head of the author of The Iliad, a work by Rembrandt van Rijn.
Aristotle Contemplating a Bust of Homer

One figure in this painting is based on the Borghese Gladiator, while the left background of this painting shows several tall white buildings behind the masts of various ships with furled sails. One person in this painting is holding a rope, which trails over the side of a boat and floats in the water. A black man with a yellow scarf is looking on in horror at the action of this painting, while three women in white shirts are comforting each other. A bald man is holding two white-shirted children over the edge of a boat in this painting, while on the right, a blue-coated man is stabbing downward with a spear towards the title animal. Identify this painting which shows the attempted rescue of a frightened youth in a Havana harbor from a violent animal, which is a work of John Copley.

A pink flamingo under a full moon is to the left of the title character in one of this man's paintings, which shows a naked woman playing a flute while a snake crawls out of a tree. In addition to The Snake Charmer, this man portrayed himself with a gigantic moustache in Self-Portrait with Lamp and showed a hawk-nosed naked woman on a couch in the middle of a jungle with huge birds in The Dream. This artist of Tiger in a Tropical Storm (Surprised!) painted two white birds on branches over dark animals in The Merry Jesters, but may be better known for a painting in which a wooden guitar lies on a sand dune under the full moon while a lion nuzzles the title person of another painting. Identify this Fauvist who painted a tired black woman in his work The Sleeping Gypsy.

This man created a film about a man who lived on top of a tower for thirty six years, an adaptation of the St. Simon story, that he renamed Simon of the Desert. Another of his films begins at a dinner party at the house of Edmundo Nobile and his wife, Lucia, and is entitled The Exterminating Angel. Two men dream of shooting the pope in his La Voie Lactee, and this man also directed Nazarin and Viridiana. This director of The Criminal Life of Archibaldo de La Cruz also directed a film based on 120 Days of Sodom, which the Duc de Blangis rapes a young girl and emerges from a room without his beard. This man may be the most well-known for collaborating with an artist to create a film in which an eye is cut, named for a Spanish animal. Identify this director of The Age of Gold and An Andalusian Dog.

This man has written several essays about the necessity of art, which include Return to Painting and The Case for Literature. This man wrote about the journal of an ecologist to a rural land to thnk about time in one of his plays, while his first play prominently features the title sound. In addition to Wild Man and Signal Alarm, this writer wrote the plays Dark City and Shelter the Rain. This man collected some novellas in the collection "Such a pigeon with red lips", while The Temple, In the Park, and The Accident appear in his short story collection A Fishing Rod for My Grandfather. This author of the play Bus Stop wrote a famous novel in which the narrator refers to himself both as he and she and after being misdiagnosed, goes to rural China to discover the title place of spiritual fulfillment. Identify this Chinese expatriate author of Soul Mountain.

This painting was referenced in Gary Tinterow's Picture for Woman, which preserves two figures from this painting and utilizes lightbulbs to give the appearance of depth. A purple and a yellow flower are in a vase in front of the central figure of this painting, and a pair of green boots drop from the upper left hand corenr of this painting, presumably belonging to a trapeze artist. A legible label for a bottle of Bass Pale Ale sits on the counter at the foreground of this painting, and a gentleman in a top hat with a brown moustache is visible to the viewer over the shoulder of a blonde haired woman in a black dress with a disinterested expression, who is at the center of this painting. Identify this painting of a drinking establishment in Paris, which was painted by Edouard Manet.

This composer rarely wrote for the piano, but his compositions for that instrument include a pair of nocturnes titled Separation and Regret. This composer of the Valse Fantasie also created a pair of pieces inspired by Spain, the Jota Aragonesa and Summer Night in Madrid. This man also collected some folk songs from his native land and created the symphonic poem Karmarinskaya. Italian influence can be seen in the arias "O, thou black night" and "O gentle autumn night", which appear in an opera in which Vanya and Antonida mourn the death of Ivan Susanin. Identify this Russian composer, who preceded The Five and wrote operas like Ruslan and Ludmila and A Life for the Tsar.

This composer's last published opus consisted of concerti musette, viela, recorder, flute, oboe or violin, and basso continuo. This composer of a notable Mandolin Concerto in C also wrote a set of violin concerti nicknamed The Extraordinary. This composer dedicated a work to Charles V, that work being his 12 violin concerti collected and nicknamed La Cetra. Four sacred works by this composer have recently been discovered in Dresden, while Fritz Kriesler improved this composer's popularity through his rediscovery. This composer's best known work is comprised of twelve movements, appeared in his set The Contest Between Harmony and Invention, and depicts actions like hunting with a horn and sitting by a fire with a plaintive violin. Nicknamed "the Red Priest", identify this Baroque composer of the set of concerti grossi The Four Seasons.

This painter published an educational guidebook, which he illustrated, entitled Quick Lessons on Simplified Drawing, and depicted Chinese subjects in works like Chinese Torture and Chinese Boys at Play. This artist portrayed several people in straw hats, including several carrying a large green box, crossing a river in Travellers Crossing the Oi River. This painter of Willow and Young Crows also depicted a sinuous fish climbing a waterfall in Carp Leaping Up a Cascade. This painter is more well-known for a work which depicts a large wave on the left which curls around a volcano and which is the first painting in his best known series. Identify this member of the ukiyo-e school who painted Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji and The Great Wave Of Kanagawa.

One movement of this piece takes its inspirtaiton from a Robert Johnson poem and utilizes a lot of the melody from Dormance. The first movement of this piece makes use of the songs Massa's in the Cold Ground and Old Black Joe, and utilizes chromaticism in the bass to evoke unreality. That movement depicts a "Black March", and also features the Reveille. Another movement in this piece utilizes instruments playing in different songs in different keys, and is intended to depict an Independence Day celebration.. Identify this work which contains the movements St. Gaudens in Boston Common, Putnam's Camp, and The Housatonic at Stockbridge, which comprise the title locations of this work by Charles Ives.

The composer of this piece later set the Agnus Dei to its music. The initial melody of this piece is restated by a lower-registered instrument, but transposed down a fifth, and is heard again in the middle section of this piece, which restates it in middle-volume cello. This piece has a coda marked by sad chords in the bass, and the melody is inverted, which leads up to the first five notes of this piece being restated slowly as the last. Marked "molto adagio espr. Cantando", this piece has a notable fortissimo climax in the highest registers of the instruments that it is scored for, and shortly after, it fades into dead silence. This piece is adapted from the first movement of the composer's earlier String Quartet Number One. Identify this "saddest ever" piece of classical music for string orchestra, which was written by Samuel Barber.

This artist created illustrations for The Crisis and Opportunity and also for James Johnson's God's Trombones. This creator of Dance Magic also illustrated works of Paul Morand with his series Black Magic. This artist created a work which shows a green gap between two orange masses with a standing saxophone player entitled Song of the Towers, while he also depicted three shadowy figures on a lavender background beholding a shining city in his work Aspiration. Those two works were part of a larger series of murals that debuted at the Schomburg Center, Aspects of Negro Life. Identify this important figure in the Harlem Renaissance, the father of African American art.

This man created a reclining brass head with a mysterious expression on its face known as the Sleeping Muse. A wide cylinder with two narrow cylinders composed in brass comprises this sculptor's Torso of a Young Man, while this man created several version of a curved spiral on a pedestal known as his Mademoiselle Pogany. This creator of the group sculptures The Table of Silence and The Gate of the Kiss also created Miastra and Newborn as part of a much more well-known series. This man also created a series of quadrahedral shapes stacked on top of one another as part of his Endless Column. Identify this sculptor of a series of sculptures that depict motion and were mistaken for farm implements, Bird in Space.

This artist of The Trench and the Trinity also depicted two versions of the same scene, one of which was entitled Modern Migration of the Spirit and the other of which was entitled Christ Destroys His Cross. This man also painted Science and a man on his knees receiving light from heaven in Omniscience Several academically clad skeletons look on as a skeleton delivers a skeleton baby from a skeleton mother in this artist's work Gods of the Modern World, which appeard as part of this artist's series in the Dartmouth library. This artist painted the three demons encircling the title immolated figure in his circular work Man on Fire, while in a better known work, he depicted the arrival of an Aztec god. Identify his muralist who painted, The Coming of Quetzalcoatl, a Mexican.

An empty bottle and one or two other small objects sit on a curved-legged wooden table in one corner of this painting, which also features a background of red drapes with a curtain pull hanging from the top of this painting. A bed at the center of this painting is covered in yellow clothes, and the red clothes on that bed spill on to the floor. The central figure of this painting wears a yellow pendant on a chain. A cow's head with inwardly lit eyes comes out of shadows at the back of this painting and looks over the shoulder of another creature in this painting. Identify this painting in which a terrifying small brown creature sits on the chest of a prostate sleeping woman in white, which is a work by Henry Fuseli.

This piece was requested by Bernard Scholz, although the composer ignored his request not to orchestrate it heavily, and Hugo Alfvén used it as inspiration for the Uppsala Rhapsody. This piece includes a bassoon solo playing "Wir hatten gebauet ein stattliches Haus", and a similar song, "Fuchslied", is also featured. The highly evocative finale of this piece utilizes the song "Gaudeamus igitur" and evokes rapture and common German drinking songs. This piece was written as a companion piece to its composer's earlier Tragic Overture. Identify this piece which was written in thanks for an honorary doctorate from the University of Breslau, which was written by Johannes Brahms.

An old woman in a blue head-scarf glares toward the viewer in this paining from the top center. An old man with a white moustache, white shirt, and a pained expression on his face sits under a panel of light on the wall of the interior scene of this painting, which is directly across from two men in top hats who are talking and staring out a window, through which can be seen hills under sky. A small child is asleep near the bottom of this painitng, and he sits next to a parcel which bears the signature of the artist as the recipient. To that child's left, a young woman in a green shirt is breastfeeding a child, and those two characters frame a wrinkly woman with a cloak with a basket. Identify this painting of the interior of the titular conveyance, which is a work by Honore Daumier.

John Barth used it in "Life Story" in Lost in the Funhouse, though some argue that it is Ambrose speaking from an extra-textual future, while Julio Cortazar used it in his stories "Graffiti" and "They Lay Down at Your Side." It can function intradiegetically or extradiegetically, based on whether or not it is used to designate a narratee on the same diegetic plane as the story or a reader who is meant to actually act. Carlos Fuentes's Aura is an example of the "complete-coincident" type, when it is actually a form of self address, as is its use in Bright Lights, Big City. Utilized prominently in Calvino's If on a Winter's Night a Traveler, FTP, name this narrative point of view associated with the pronoun "you."

After completing his Masters in architecture, he spent ten years working for Eero Saarinen, for whom he was project designer for the TWA Terminal at JFK Airport. The designer of the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo, the Yale Music Center in New Haven, and the Residential Tower of the Museum of Modern Art, this architect believes that buildings should be both background and foreground, as well as "responsible citizens." For ten points name this Argentinian-born UIUC grad and designer of the Petronas Towers.

The original theme of the Scherzo of this work was found in the Dictionnaire de la musique under Chinese Music. The Andantino was originally a piano duet and the Finale is a majestic march. Based on music written for a ballet commissioned by Massine, it begins with a Viennese march interrupted by the Turandot Overture. Written by a German political refugee in America, it became the greatest set of variations in twentieth century music. Name this Paul Hindemith translation of the music by the composer of Der Freischutz.
Symphonic Metamorphosis of Themes by Carl Maria von Weber

The protagonist of this film hatches the idea for his final crime during a performance of Schubert's Unfinished Symphony at the Hollywood Bowl, on a date with Lola. Enticed by honeysuckle perfume, he cannot get off the trolley ride until the end of the line where the cemetery is. Cutting it straight down the line with Phyllis, Walter lights cigars for Keyes until the very end. Name this Billy Wilder film-noir in which an insurance salesman confesses.

This artist married Susan Hannah MacDowell, who was an accomplished pianist, photographer, and painter at the time. The Corcoran houses his full- length portrait The Pathetic Song, which perhaps falls behind his portraits Mary Adeline Williams and Miss Van Buren. After his return to America, he began to employ Muybridge's photographic researches in his paintings, which ended an early hobby that could be seen in such canvases as The Biglen Brothers Racing and Max Schmitt in a Single Scull. FTP, name this American painter whose fascination with anatomy is best expressed in his masterpiece, The Gross Clinic.

Instead of directly setting the text of the central prayer to music, the composer interpreted it sonically in the final movement of this work. Opening with a gong, the bass establishes the four-note theme that climaxes in a chant to end the first movement. Nominally a four-part suite for quartet, its concluding sections, "Persuance" and "Psalm", form a continuum. Stylistically influenced by the Free Jazz of Ornette Coleman, its definitive recording featured McCoy Tyner on piano and its composer on tenor saxophone. What was this spiritual 1964 work of John Coltrane?

A dog peeks its head up over a ridge to stare into a foreboding orange sky in this series of works, while the depiction of the Fates includes an unidentified fourth figure. In another of them, the artist's lover, Leocadia, leans on a grave rail and the artist represents himself as a deaf old man being shouted at by another. Two of the more horrific images are that of a satanic goat leading a witches' sabbath and of Saturn devouring his children. Executed directly upon the whitewashed walls of the two-story house Quinta del Sordo, name this series of fourteen dark paintings by Francisco Goya.

Notre-Dame de Paris is barely visible in the upper right, and the artist himself appears in a top hat on the far left. Behind him, a peasant with a cutlass stands poised to attack; in front of him, two men lay dying, victims of the 1830 event that the artist meant to commemorate. This painting's most notable image, however, is the bare-breasted Marianne waving the tricolor in its center. FTP, name this painting of the July Revolution by Eugene Delacroix.

This artist began his career as a caricaturist and then moved on to landscape painting under the advice of his mentor Boudin. He became fond of painting outdoors and, after two years in Algiers with the military, moved to Paris to become a member of the studio Gleyre. He had a trench dug in his garden so that the overlarge Women in the Garden could be raised or lowered to a height that he liked. Name this archetypal artist of the Impressionist movement, famous for painting Impression: Sunrise.

This painting contains allusions to Baron Gros's Napoleon at Eylau and Fuseli's Count Ugolino, a hint at the activities preceding the depicted scene, and incorporates material from the artist's earlier Beaujon Hospital Studies. The likenesses of Correard and Savigny, as well as the ship Argus appear in earlier incarnations of this painting in which three figures at center pull themselves to their feet away from the dead and dying, while three men mount barrels and signal to the right with unfurled cloths. For ten points name this famous painting depicting an ad-hoc lifeboat off Senegal, a work of Theodore Gericault.

Pravda attacked his Saxophone Concerto in E Flat Major for "bourgeois decadence" just before his death, preventing him from hearing it performed. His contributions to the national styles of neighboring cultures include two Overtures on Three Greek Themes, and a set of "Finnish Sketches." His influence on Russian style began with his symphonic poems "Stenka Razin" and "The Kremlin." He helped to complete the arias for Prince Igor and orchestrated Chopin's piano music for the ballet Les Sylphides. Name this Russian composer perhaps best remembered for his ballet The Seasons.

Beethoven's Opus 84, its introduction is a musical duel between a heavy passage in F-minor and a menacing sarabande. Its central woodwind section leads to a pause from which the allegro passage "Victory Symphony" emerges. It is the only surviving piece from a 10-part program for a work of Goethe.

In this work, painted for the ceiling of a room of Egyptian antiquities in the Louvre, two statuesque females, one holding a dagger and the other resting an oar on her lap, sit at the feet of the title figure. Figures in the foreground include Poussin, Shakespeare, Racine, Moliere, and Voltaire. To the title figure's right are Horace, Virgil, Dante and Rafael, from whose painting School of Athens the artist got his idea for the work, while an Ionic temple looms in the background. Identify the Ingres work in which Victory crowns the titular Greek bard.

John Eccles composed operas based on this man's libretti for The Judgment of Paris and Semele. His later works include the poems Tears of Amaryllis for Amyntas and A Pindarique Ode as well as a translation of Moliere's Monsieur de Pourceaugnac. His second play, The Double Dealer, was far less successful than his first, The Old Bachelor. His only tragedy was The Mourning Bride, from which comes the line "Nor hell to a woman scorned." His two most famous works concern Valentine's attempt to regain his inheritance and Mirabell's attempts to snag Millamant. Identify this Restoration dramatist of Love for Love and The Way of the World.

The second piece in this musical work is scored for orchestra in four movements, each with two titles, such as "Prelude/Song of the Hoodlum" and "Toccata/The Little Train to Caipira". Consisting of 9 compositions scored for various media, the most famous is probably the fifth, written for soprano and cello octet, consisting of a wordless chant surrounding a setting of a Brazilian folk song. Seeking to combine elements of Brazilian folk music with the contrapuntal style of J.S. Bach, what is this work by Heitor Villa-Lobos?

Physical violence can be seen breaking out among two men on the far right of this painting, the oldest-known fresco for which a preliminary sketch survives. The scene is dominated by the huge triumphal arch in the top left, drawn to account for the viewer's intending position below and to the right of the painting. The greatest of the paintings of the Church of the Eremitani that were almost totally destroyed by a bomb in 1944, its main action occurs on the left, where a paralytic is commanded to walk by the half-brother of Jesus. What is this painting by Andrea Mantegna?
St. James Led to His Execution

This man spent most of his later years designing a wooden glider based on insect forms. Beginning as an icon painter, after meeting Picasso in 1913 he incorporated Cubism into works like his series of 4 three-dimensional painted Reliefs. His "Programme of the Productivist Group" saw the origins of a state- sanctioned artistic group that worked on utilitarian furniture and housing. When his most famous design was finished in 1920, it consisted of an iron spiral framework containing a glass cylinder, cone, and cube. That work was intended to be twice as tall as the Empire State Building, but Mother Russia characteristically lacked the steel. For ten points identify the artist who, after designing his "Monument to the Third International," became the leader of the Constructivists.

Arias in this opera include "Recondita Armonia", "E Lucevan de Stelle", and "Vissi d'arte, vissi d'amore", the last of which is by the title character. The fair-haired Marchesa Attavanti is recognized in a painting, after which the political prisoner Angelotti reveals his identity, and as a result is pursued by Scarpia, whose jealous love for the title character leads to his first torture and then execution of her lover, Mario Cavaradossi. She then stabs Scarpia and jumps off the battlements to her death. FTP, name this opera by Giacomo Puccini.

In a joke in this dialogue, Socrates says that his ever-changing definitions can be attributed to descent from Daedelus, whose sculptures were said to change shape on their own. The title character is caught substituting an example for a definition, and his final assertion about actions which please all of the gods is shown to be a tautology. Socrates, who is seeking help in his upcoming trial, proposes that "the part of justice concerned with care of the gods" is the nature of the central concept. This work takes place on the porch of the King Archon, where the title character is bringing charges against his father for killing a servant. Name this Platonic dialogue which attempts to define piety.

Several of his principal works contain dances which were later arranged separately, such as "The Miller's Wife" and "Ritual Fire Dance." Halffter finished his epic "scenic cantata" Atlántida. His studies with Pedrell convinced him that the spirit of folk song should influence a nation's music, and he put the idea to work in the opera The Brief Life and the ballet The Love Wizard. He then drew on Don Quixote for the chamber opera Master Peter's Puppet Show and on the guitar for the Homage to Debussy. Name this composer of Nights in the Gardens of Spain and The Three-Cornered Hat.
Manuel Maria de Falla y Matheu

The finale, which requires an "eleventh finger." is based on the folk wedding tune "Grandfather's Dance." Each piece is a roman á clef representing such figures as Ernestine von Fricken, Chopin, Paganini, and Beethoven. Inspired by the masked ball in Richter's novel Age of Indiscretion, this set of twelve dance pieces for the piano is not intended to depict the title creatures but rather represent the composer's artistic metamorphosis. Name this lepidopterous work of Robert Schumann.

He composed Half-Mast Inhibition at age seventeen, although it was not performed until his reputation was already established with Revelations. Another gap, of ten years, passed between his 1979 death from ALS and the performance of his two-hour piece Epitaph. Scholars debate whether his "Better git it in your soul" or Miles Davis's "All Blues" was the first use of 3/4 time in jazz. His albums included Tijuana Moods, Pithecanthropus Erectus, The Clown, and Let My Children Hear Music. Name this musician who injected leading melodies into the previously rhythmic role of the upright bass.

Jane Brown separates this movement from its predecessor by noting its pessimism at the subject-object dichotomy in works like "In the Lovely Month of May." Among the lyrics it produced were "Reed Songs" and "To an Old painting," while longer works associated with it are The Spiritual Year and Wisdom of the Brahmins. In addition to Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, Eduard Morike and Friedrich Ruckert, it is associated with a poem about a fisherman who looks at a golden goddess instead of the deadly rocks around him, "Die Lorelei," which was collected in The Book of Songs. The source of many song cycles, FTP, name this post-Romantic German movement at its peak between 1815-1848, exemplified by Heinrich Heine.

One character in this work sings a lewd song that involves lots of rapping on a table, alternately attributed to the Dean of the Harvard Divinity School, Ralph Waldo Emerson, and Jonathan Edwards. One character is convinced that crickets will frighten another when he buys a farm, and another character often says "the days grow hot, O Babylon" and addresses others as "leedle monkey-faces." Major characters include Boer War adversaries Lewis and Wetjoen, and one-time gambling-house owner Joe Mott. Don Parritt commits suicide at this work's end, but only "foolosopher" and former anarchist Larry Slade notices. FTP, name this play in which the denizens of Harry Hope's bar temporarily give up their pipe dreams on the advice of Theodore "Hickey" Hickman, a work of Eugene O'Neill.

In Orientalism, Edward Said contrasts this work's positive treatment of Saladin with its scatologically-accurate depiction of Mohammed's bisection. The narrator of this work encounters the madman Phlyegas, the parodic hymnist Plutus, a blind man who asks if his poet son Guido is dead, and the general Farinata. At age thirty-five, that narrator, awakes to find himself in the Dark Wood of Error in its first tercet, from whence he asks to be led to Peter's grave and soon encounters a a stone reading "I am the way into the City of Woe…Abandon all hope ye who enter here." FTP, name this first part of the The Divine Comedy, where Virgil leads Dante through Hell.

According to the art historian Edgar Wind, the inspiration for this painting was Hogarth's depiction of David Garrick. Another art historian, Marco Beretta, has argued that the objects depicted on the right side of this painting fol ow the chronological progression in which they were employed by one of this painting's subjects. In the left center background of this painting is a folio, intended to hint at the artistic profession of one of the figures depicted in this painting, who had previously been a pupil of the artist. The first title figure of this work is depicted writing with a quil as he sits at a table covered with a red cloth, and looks over his right shoulder at the second title figure, who wears a dress tied with a blue sash and leans on her partner's shoulder. Also depicted in this painting are numerous glass implements, such as a bel jar and a large flask on the ground. Identify this painting by Jacques-Louis David which depicts a famous chemist and the woman he married.
Portrait of Atoine-Laurent Lavoisier and His Wife, Marie-Anne Pierette Paulze

One painting by this artist depicts the title winged creature with its paw resting on a book opened to face the viewer; that painting, set against a Venetian background, is this artist's The Lion of St. Mark. This artist's series for the Scuola di San Giorgio degli Schiavoni depicts episodes in the life of St. Jerome, St. Trifon, and of course St. George, the latter of whom is depicted baptizing the Selenites in one panel. The subject of this artist's most famous series is depicted sleeping in a canopied bed on the left as an angel enters from the right bearing news of her martyrdom in one work, and also depicted the title figures being glorified at the top of the title landmark in his monumental The Crucifixion and Glorification of 10,000 Martyrs on Mt. Ararat. This artist's most famous work was inspired by the Golden Legend of Jacopo da Varagine, and consists of a set of nine large paintings which tel the story of a Christian saint martyred by Attila the Hun along with 10,000 virgins. Identify this Venetian Renaissance painter best known for his series of the life and martyrdom of St. Ursula.
